newsitem.title: THAILAND: New Thai government urged to adopt disciplines.
newsitem.headline: New Thai government urged to adopt disciplines.

text.p: Economists and former finance ministers on Wednesday urged the new Thai government emerging from the Sunday general election to be honest and serious in adopting financial disciplines.

Former finance minister Virabongsa Ramankura said at a function that Thailand should not expect that problems of its economic slowdown and sharply lower export growth would be solved by an imaginary white knight.

"We cannot wait for a white knight to show up in the time ahead. What we need is for Thailand to build a buffer that would boost our economic resilience to help us withstand any further economic shocks," he said.

Virabongsa's comments were aimed at an economic team being formed by caretaker defence minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, tipped to be the next prime minister after his New Aspiration Party (NAP) captured the largest number of seats in the 393-seat lower House of Representatives on Sunday.
The Thai economy is projected to grow about six to seven percent in 1996, its slowest pace in 10 years and against 8.6 percent in 1995.
Exports are expected to rise only three to four percent this year against an average 20 percent in each of the past five years.
Paichitr Uathaweekul, another former finance minister in the 1980s, said the new government must be honest and serious in implementing financial disciplines.
"The new government must be honest and not let the current crisis of confidence (in the government) be aggravated by corruption," he said.

The caretaker coalition of Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa was accused by critics and the opposition of economic mismanagement and excessive fiscal spending on infrastructure during its 15-month tenure.

Paichitr asked the Chavalit-led government not to meddle in economic and financial policies set by the Bank of Thailand and the government think tank National Economic and Social Development Board (NESDB).

Chavalit pledged during his election campaign that, if elected, he would appoint an economic "dream team" led by caretaker deputy premier and former banker Amnuay Viravan to help reverse economic slowdown.

But analysts said demands on economic ministerial jobs made by Chavalit's five coalition partners may hamper the NAP leader's efforts to recruit non-elected economists to join his cabinet, expected to be announced in early December.
Former premier Anand Panyarachun reminded businessmen at the same function that Chavalit's economic dream team was a campaign slogan that should not be taken seriously after the poll.
He said what the country needs is a good and smoothly functioning government.
